Matching Multi-Loop Complexities with a Single Loop: Optimal Optimization Stationarity and Best-Known Game Stationarity in Nonconvex–Concave Minimax Optimization

Minhao Zhang Email: zhangminhao@shu.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, College of Sciences, Shanghai University, Shanghai, 200444, P.R.China    Zi Xu Email: xuzi@shu.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, College of Sciences, Shanghai University, Shanghai, 200444, P.R.China
Abstract

We introduce a new single-loop algorithmic framework for smooth nonconvex–concave minimax optimization. The resulting projected damped extragradient method combines projected extragradient updates, dual momentum, and a moving proximal center. Under both the optimization- stationarity and game-stationarity criteria, our method achieves the best-known complexity among single-loop first-order methods. For optimization stationarity, our method achieves a gradient complexity of 𝒪⁡(L2​DY​Δ¯0​ε−3)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}D_{Y}\bar{\Delta}_{0}\varepsilon^{-3}), where LL is the gradient Lipschitz constant, DYD_{Y} bounds the diameter of the dual feasible set, and Δ¯0\bar{\Delta}_{0} is an initialization quantity involving the value-function gap and the initial gradients. Moreover, by incorporating a fixed-center warm-up phase, the complexity can be improved to 𝒪⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}), up to an additive lower-order cost, where Δϕ:=ϕ⁡(x0)−infxϕ⁡(x)\Delta_{\phi}:=\phi(x_{0})-\inf_{x}\phi(x). We further establish a lower bound of Ω⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3)\Omega(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}) for optimization stationarity over projected zero-respecting first-order methods. This lower bound proves that the warm-started version of our algorithm is optimal up to a constant factor for optimization stationarity within this oracle class. For game stationarity, our method achieves 𝒪(L3/2DY1/2Δϕε−5/2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(L^{3/2}D_{Y}^{1/2}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-5/2}\right) gradient complexity. This matches the best-known complexity of multi-loop first-order methods, thereby establishing the same complexity with a single-loop algorithmic structure. Under dual strong concavity, the proposed framework achieves 𝒪⁡(κ​L​Δϕ​ε−2)\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}\,L\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-2}\right) leading complexity for both stationarity criteria, where κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu is the dual condition number, up to an additive initialization cost. The ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} accuracy dependence is optimal under fixed regularity and initialization bounds.

keywords
Minimax optimization, Nonconvex optimization, Single-loop methods, Extragradient methods, Oracle complexity, Lyapunov analysis

1 Introduction

We study the deterministic nonconvex–concave (NC–C) minimax problem

minx∈X⁡maxy∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y),\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y),

where XX is nonempty, closed, and convex, YY is nonempty, compact, and convex, and ff has an LL-Lipschitz continuous gradient. The objective is possibly nonconvex in xx and concave in yy. Smooth instances arise in distributionally robust learning Rafique et al. (2022), group robust learning Sagawa et al. (2020), and learning with average top-kk losses Fan et al. (2017). In these applications, the dual variable weights samples or groups, or selects large losses, while the primal variable parametrizes a possibly nonconvex model. A central algorithmic challenge is to attain sharp stationarity guarantees using simple first-order updates, without repeatedly solving auxiliary optimization problems.

Two stationarity criteria are relevant to this problem. Optimization stationarity (OS) measures the gradient of a Moreau envelope of the value function ϕ⁡(x)=maxy∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y)\phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y), extended by +∞+\infty outside XX. Game stationarity (GS) measures the joint first-order residual of ff, including the normal cones to XX and YY. These criteria capture different aspects of stationarity and must also be distinguished from the value-gradient and projected-gradient-mapping criteria used in earlier works. Their formal definitions are given in Section 2. In the literature review below, complexity bounds suppress fixed smoothness, domain, and initialization quantities unless displayed explicitly; O~\widetilde{O} additionally suppresses logarithmic factors.

Dual strong concavity provides an important point of comparison. In the nonconvex–strongly concave (NC–SC) setting, let μ>0\mu>0 be the strong concavity parameter and write κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu. For an unconstrained primal variable, two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TS-GDA) attains O⁡(κ2​ε−2)O(\kappa^{2}\varepsilon^{-2}) complexity for value-gradient stationarity Lin et al. (2020b); Lin et al. (2025). Under a dual Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition on unconstrained domains, Smoothed-AGDA improves the dependence to O⁡(κ​ε−2)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-2}) for GS, with a terminal refinement giving the same leading order for value-gradient stationarity Yang et al. (2022). Minimax-PPA and Catalyst-EG/OGDA attain O~​(κ​ε−2)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon^{-2}) complexity under strong concavity Lin et al. (2020a); Zhang et al. (2021). The single-loop mirror descent ascent method MDA also reports O⁡(κ​ε−2)O(\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon^{-2}) complexity under its prescribed mirror geometry and mirror-gradient-mapping criterion Huang et al. (2021). Lower bounds of Ω⁡(κ​L​Δϕ​ε−2)\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-2}) are known for value-gradient stationarity in the corresponding unconstrained oracle models Li et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2021), where Δϕ=ϕ⁡(x0)−infx∈Xϕ⁡(x)\Delta_{\phi}=\phi(x_{0})-\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x).

The general NC–C setting is more difficult because the value function can be nonsmooth. Multi-loop methods address this difficulty by solving auxiliary optimization problems. Prox-DIAG Thekumparampil et al. (2019) and Minimax-PPA Lin et al. (2020a) attain O~​(ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}) complexity for OS. Minimax-PPA also gives O~(ε−5/2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-5/2}) complexity under its game-stationarity formulation. Li et al. Li et al. (2026) develop Perturbed Smoothed FOAM, which attains O~​(ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}) for OS and O~(ε−5/2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-5/2}) for GS. These methods obtain their guarantees through regularized strongly convex–strongly concave subproblems, whose solution requires inner iterations.

Single-loop methods use a fixed number of elementary first-order updates per iteration, but their representative NC–C guarantees have been weaker. TS-GDA has an O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) OS bound under an additional primal Lipschitz assumption Lin et al. (2020b); Lin et al. (2025), while AGP attains O⁡(ε−4)O(\varepsilon^{-4}) under a projected primal–dual gradient-mapping criterion on compact convex domains Xu et al. (2023). The analysis of Li et al. Li et al. (2026) establishes O⁡(ε−4)O(\varepsilon^{-4}) complexity for Smoothed GDA under both OS and GS. Their Perturbed Smoothed GDA improves the GS bound to O⁡(ε−3)O(\varepsilon^{-3}), while retaining an O⁡(ε−4)O(\varepsilon^{-4}) OS bound. Thus, under both criteria, a complexity gap remains between these single-loop methods and methods that rely on auxiliary solvers. This motivates the following question:

Can a single-loop first-order method attain the best-known multi-loop complexity rates under both OS and GS, and can its complexity be certified as optimal by a matching lower bound?

We answer the algorithmic question affirmatively under both stationarity criteria and establish a matching lower bound for OS. Our method achieves the best-known complexity among single-loop first-order methods under both OS and GS. Its warm-started OS complexity is optimal up to a constant factor within the projected zero-respecting first-order oracle class, while its GS complexity matches the best-known rate of multi-loop first-order methods. The same framework also attains the sharp O⁡(κ​ε−2)O(\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon^{-2}) dependence under dual strong concavity. Our contributions are as follows; DYD_{Y} denotes an upper bound on the dual diameter.

  1. 1.

    A new single-loop algorithm and Lyapunov analysis. We develop a projected damped extragradient framework combining projected prediction–correction steps, dual momentum, and a moving proximal center. A new joint Lyapunov function couples descent of a regularized envelope with tracking of its saddle point, allowing both effects to be controlled within a single loop. A predetermined fixed-center warm-up reduces the initialization dependence while using the same elementary updates, without resetting the state or introducing repeated inner solves.

  2. 2.

    Optimal OS complexity and a matching lower bound. For NC–C problems, the method achieves gradient complexity

    O⁡(L2​DY​Δ¯0​ε−3),O\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\bar{\Delta}_{0}\varepsilon^{-3}\right),

    where Δ¯0\bar{\Delta}_{0} involves the initial value-function gap and initial gradients. The fixed-center warm-up improves this bound to

    O⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3),O\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}\right),

    up to an additive lower-order cost, with an expected squared Moreau-gradient guarantee (Corollary 4.3). We also prove the lower bound

    Ω⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3)\Omega\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}\right)

    for projected zero-respecting first-order methods, including randomized output rules at a fixed query budget (Theorem 5.1). The upper and lower bounds match in their dependence on LL, DYD_{Y}, Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, and ε\varepsilon, establishing optimality up to a constant factor for the leading warm-started OS complexity within this oracle class.

  3. 3.

    Multi-loop GS complexity attained with a single loop. For NC–C problems, the warm-started method returns a deterministic best-certificate iterate with leading gradient complexity

    O(L3/2DY1/2Δϕε−5/2),O\!\left(L^{3/2}D_{Y}^{1/2}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-5/2}\right),

    with an additive lower-order warm-up cost (Corollary 4.4). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first single-loop method to attain the best-known ε−5/2\varepsilon^{-5/2} GS complexity of multi-loop first-order methods for general smooth NC–C problems. The leading term has no multiplicative logarithmic factor.

  4. 4.

    A common framework for the strongly concave case. Under dual strong concavity, the same framework requires no dual perturbation and yields O⁡(κ​L​Δ0​ε−2)O(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}) complexity for both OS and GS, where Δ0\Delta_{0} is the corresponding initialization quantity. With the fixed-center warm-up, the leading complexity becomes

    O⁡(κ​L​Δϕ​ε−2)O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-2}\right)

    for fixed problem and initialization quantities with Δϕ>0\Delta_{\phi}>0 as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 (Corollary 4.2). This dependence matches the known NC–SC lower-bound rate for value-gradient stationarity in the corresponding unconstrained oracle models.

Table 1 compares our NC–C upper bounds with representative single- and multi-loop first-order methods and records the OS lower bound established in this paper.

Organization. Section 2 states the assumptions and stationarity criteria. Section 3 presents the algorithm. Section 4 develops the common Lyapunov analysis and establishes the NC–SC and NC–C complexity bounds, together with the warm-up refinement. Section 5 proves the matching OS lower bound and specifies the oracle class in which the leading warm-started complexity is optimal. Section 6 presents numerical illustrations, and Section 7 concludes. The appendices contain the technical proofs.

Notation. We use ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle and ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert for the Euclidean inner product and norm, respectively, with ∥(x,y)∥2=∥x∥2+∥y∥2\lVert(x,y)\rVert^{2}=\lVert x\rVert^{2}+\lVert y\rVert^{2} on product spaces. For matrices, ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert denotes the spectral norm. For a nonempty closed convex set C⊆ℝdC\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, let ΠC​(w):=argminu∈C∥u−w∥2/2\Pi_{C}(w):=\argmin_{u\in C}\lVert u-w\rVert^{2}/2 be the Euclidean projection onto CC, and let NC​(u):={η∈ℝd:⟨η,a−u⟩≤0​ for all ​a∈C}N_{C}(u):=\{\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle\eta,a-u\rangle\leq 0\text{ for all }a\in C\} be its normal cone at u∈Cu\in C. For a nonempty set SS, write dist⁡(w,S):=infu∈S∥w−u∥\dist(w,S):=\inf_{u\in S}\lVert w-u\rVert and diam⁡(S):=supu,v∈S∥u−v∥\diam(S):=\sup_{u,v\in S}\lVert u-v\rVert. The support of a vector uu is supp⁡(u):={i:ui≠0}\supp(u):=\{i:u_{i}\neq 0\}, and 𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes expectation over all randomness.

2 Problem Formulation and Preliminaries

2.1 Problem setting and assumptions

We consider the deterministic minimax problem

minx∈X⁡maxy∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y),\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y), (2.1)

where X⊆ℝnX\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is nonempty, closed, and convex, and Y⊆ℝpY\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} is nonempty, compact, and convex. Let DY>0D_{Y}>0 be an upper bound on the diameter of YY. After a translation of the dual coordinates, we assume 0∈Y0\in Y, so that ∥y∥≤DY\lVert y\rVert\leq D_{Y} for every y∈Yy\in Y.

Assumption 2.1.

The function ff is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of X×YX\times Y and satisfies the following conditions.

  1. (i)

    For some L>0L>0 and all (x,y),(x′,y′)∈X×Y(x,y),(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in X\times Y,

    ∥∇f​(x′,y′)−∇f​(x,y)∥≤L⁡∥(x′−x,y′−y)∥.\lVert\nabla f(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})-\nabla f(x,y)\rVert\leq L\lVert(x^{\prime}-x,y^{\prime}-y)\rVert. (2.2)
  2. (ii)

    For some 0≤μ≤L0\leq\mu\leq L, the function f⁡(x,⋅)f(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly concave on YY for every x∈Xx\in X; namely,

    f⁡(x,y′)≤f⁡(x,y)+⟨∇yf​(x,y),y′−y⟩−μ2​∥y′−y∥2,y,y′∈Y.{f(x,y^{\prime})\leq f(x,y)+\langle\nabla_{y}f(x,y),y^{\prime}-y\rangle-\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert y^{\prime}-y\rVert^{2},\qquad y,y^{\prime}\in Y.} (2.3)
  3. (iii)

    The value function is bounded below:

    infx∈Xmaxy∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y)>−∞.\inf_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)>-\infty. (2.4)

Define the extended-valued value function of (2.1) by

ϕ⁡(x)={maxy∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y),x∈X,+∞,x∉X.\phi(x)=\begin{cases}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y),&x\in X,\\ +\infty,&x\notin X.\end{cases} (2.5)

By (2.4), we have ϕinf:=infx∈Xϕ⁡(x)>−∞\phi_{\inf}:=\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x)>-\infty. When μ>0\mu>0, the maximizer over YY is unique and the finite-valued mapping x↦maxy∈Y⁡f⁡(x,y)x\mapsto\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y) is differentiable at every x∈Xx\in X. When μ=0\mu=0, this mapping may be nonsmooth even though ff is smooth, motivating the use of the Moreau envelope to study stationarity. For λ>L\lambda>L, define the Moreau envelope and proximal mapping of ϕ\phi by

Φλ​(z)\displaystyle\Phi_{\lambda}(z) =minx∈X⁡{ϕ⁡(x)+λ2​∥x−z∥2},\displaystyle=\min_{x\in X}\left\{\phi(x)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\right\}, (2.6)
x¯​(z)\displaystyle\bar{x}(z) =proxϕ/λ⁡(z)=argminx∈X{ϕ⁡(x)+λ2​∥x−z∥2}.\displaystyle=\operatorname{prox}_{\phi/\lambda}(z)=\argmin_{x\in X}\left\{\phi(x)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\right\}. (2.7)

The function ϕ\phi is LL-weakly convex. Thus the minimizer in (2.7) is unique and

∇Φλ​(z)=λ⁡(z−x¯​(z)).\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z)=\lambda\bigl(z-\bar{x}(z)\bigr). (2.8)

For properties of the value function ϕ\phi and its Moreau envelope Φλ\Phi_{\lambda}, see Lin et al. (2025).

2.2 Stationarity measures

We use two stationarity criteria for (2.1): optimization stationarity (OS), based on the Moreau envelope of the value function, and game stationarity (GS), based on first-order residuals in both variables.

Definition 2.1 (ε\varepsilon-optimization stationary point).

For λ>L\lambda>L and ε>0\varepsilon>0, a point x∈Xx\in X is an ε\varepsilon-optimization stationary point relative to λ\lambda if

∥∇Φλ​(x)∥≤ε.\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon. (2.9)

A random point Z∈XZ\in X almost surely is ε\varepsilon-optimization stationary in expectation relative to λ\lambda if

𝔼⁡∥∇Φλ​(Z)∥≤ε.\mathbb{E}\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(Z)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

The OS upper bounds below establish the stronger guarantee 𝔼​∥∇Φλ​(Z)∥2≤ε2\mathbb{E}\lVert\nabla\Phi_{{\lambda}}(Z)\rVert^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}, which implies this expected-norm criterion by Jensen’s inequality.

For game stationarity, define the residual at (x,y)∈X×Y(x,y)\in X\times Y by

ℛ⁡(x,y)=dist2⁡(0,∇xf​(x,y)+NX​(x))+dist2⁡(0,−∇yf​(x,y)+NY​(y)).{\mathcal{R}(x,y)=\sqrt{\dist^{2}\bigl(0,\nabla_{x}f(x,y)+N_{X}(x)\bigr)+\dist^{2}\bigl(0,-\nabla_{y}f(x,y)+N_{Y}(y)\bigr)}.} (2.10)
Definition 2.2 (ε\varepsilon-game stationary point).

For ε>0\varepsilon>0, a pair (x,y)∈X×Y(x,y)\in X\times Y is an ε\varepsilon-game stationary point of (2.1) if

ℛ⁡(x,y)≤ε.\mathcal{R}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon. (2.11)

For further discussion of these stationarity criteria and their relationships, see Lin et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026).

3 Algorithm

3.1 Regularized saddle-point formulation

We first introduce a regularized saddle-point problem. Fix λ>L\lambda>L and choose τ≥0\tau\geq 0 such that μy:=μ+τ>0\mu_{y}:=\mu+\tau>0. For a center z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define

p⁡(z)=minx∈X⁡maxy∈Y⁡G⁡(x,y,z),p(z)=\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}G(x,y;z), (3.1)

where

G⁡(x,y,z)=f⁡(x,y)+λ2​∥x−z∥2−τ2​∥y∥2.G(x,y;z)=f(x,y)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}-\frac{\tau}{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}.

The function G⁡(⋅,⋅,z)G(\cdot,\cdot;z) is (λ−L)(\lambda-L)-strongly convex in xx and μy\mu_{y}-strongly concave in yy, so the auxiliary problem has a unique saddle point (x⋆​(z),y⋆​(z))(x^{\star}(z),y^{\star}(z)). Write G⋆​(z)=G⁡(x⋆​(z),y⋆​(z),z)=p⁡(z)G^{\star}(z)=G(x^{\star}(z),y^{\star}(z);z)=p(z). The envelope is continuously differentiable and

∇p​(z)=λ⁡(z−x⋆​(z)).\nabla p(z)=\lambda\bigl(z-x^{\star}(z)\bigr). (3.2)

For this regularized formulation and its envelope properties, see (Li et al., 2026, Sections 3.1 and 6). If τ=0\tau=0, then p=Φλp=\Phi_{\lambda}. Positive τ\tau supplies the dual curvature needed when the original problem is merely concave. The same auxiliary problem is used by Li et al. Li et al. (2026), whereas our method employs different primal–dual updates and a different Lyapunov function.

3.2 Algorithm and implementation

We now use the regularized saddle-point formulation (3.1) to construct a single-loop method. At iteration tt, with z=ztz=z_{t} fixed, we apply a projected extragradient step with dual momentum: a prediction is followed by a correction using gradients at the predicted pair. We then update ztz_{t} toward the corrected primal iterate xt+1x_{t+1}. The complete procedure is presented in Algorithm 1.

The subproblem iteration is a modified version of the damped extragradient method developed in our unpublished manuscript on unconstrained strongly convex–strongly concave minimax optimization. To handle the constraints XX and YY, we introduce projections and the normal-cone variables ξt\xi_{t} and ntn_{t}. The dual correction ntn_{t} enters both the prediction and momentum updates. The following lemma shows that these variables belong to the normal cones at the corresponding iterates.

Lemma 3.1.

The iterates of Algorithm 1 satisfy

ξt∈NX(xt),nt∈NY(yt),t=0,…,T.\xi_{t}\in N_{X}(x_{t}),\qquad n_{t}\in N_{Y}(y_{t}),\qquad t=0,\ldots,T. (3.3)
Proof.

At initialization, both normal-cone inequalities hold because ξ0=n0=0\xi_{0}=n_{0}=0. For any x∈Xx\in X, the projection theorem applied to the primal correction gives

⟨xt−xt+1h−∇xf​(x~t,y~t)−λ⁡(x~t−zt),x−xt+1⟩≤0.\left\langle\frac{x_{t}-x_{t+1}}{h}-\nabla_{x}f(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t})-\lambda(\widetilde{x}_{t}-z_{t}),\,x-x_{t+1}\right\rangle\leq 0.

By the definition of ξt+1\xi_{t+1}, this is ⟨ξt+1,x−xt+1⟩≤0\langle\xi_{t+1},x-x_{t+1}\rangle\leq 0. Similarly, for any y∈Yy\in Y, the dual projection gives

⟨yt−yt+1h+∇yf​(x~t,y~t)−τ​y~t+v¯t,y−yt+1⟩≤0.\left\langle\frac{y_{t}-y_{t+1}}{h}+\nabla_{y}f(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t})-\tau\widetilde{y}_{t}+\bar{v}_{t},\,y-y_{t+1}\right\rangle\leq 0.

The first argument is [1+(1−α)​γ]​nt+1[1+(1-\alpha)\gamma]n_{t+1}. Since 1+(1−α)​γ>01+(1-\alpha)\gamma>0, division yields ⟨nt+1,y−yt+1⟩≤0\langle n_{t+1},y-y_{t+1}\rangle\leq 0. As x∈Xx\in X and y∈Yy\in Y are arbitrary, these inequalities prove ξt+1∈NX​(xt+1)\xi_{t+1}\in N_{X}(x_{t+1}) and nt+1∈NY​(yt+1)n_{t+1}\in N_{Y}(y_{t+1}). ∎

To implement the game-stationarity output in Algorithm 1, define the computable certificate at each corrected iterate by

St=∥∇xf​(xt+1,yt+1)+ξt+1∥2+∥−∇yf​(xt+1,yt+1)+τ​yt+1+nt+1∥2.S_{t}=\lVert\nabla_{x}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+\xi_{t+1}\rVert^{2}+\lVert-\nabla_{y}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+\tau y_{t+1}+n_{t+1}\rVert^{2}. (3.4)

The quantity StS_{t} is the squared norm of a stationarity residual for the dual-regularized objective f⁡(x,y)−τ​∥y∥2/2f(x,y)-\tau\lVert y\rVert^{2}/2, evaluated using the normal-cone vectors supplied by the algorithm. It is used to select the game-stationarity output. The following lemma relates this certificate and the auxiliary envelope gradient to the stationarity measures of the original problem. Its proof is given in Appendix 10.1.

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose that Assumption 2.1 holds, τ≥0\tau\geq 0, λ>L\lambda>L, and μ+τ>0\mu+\tau>0. Then the iterates of Algorithm 1 satisfy

ℛ⁡(xt+1,yt+1)≤St+τ​DY\mathcal{R}(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})\leq\sqrt{S_{t}}+\tau D_{Y} (3.5)

Moreover, for every z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

‖∇Φλ​(z)−∇p​(z)‖≤λ​DY​τλ−L.\|\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z)-\nabla p(z)\|\leq\lambda D_{Y}\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\lambda-L}}. (3.6)

Consequently, for every iterate ztz_{t},

‖∇Φλ​(zt)‖≤‖∇p​(zt)‖+λ​DY​τλ−L.\|\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z_{t})\|\leq\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|+\lambda D_{Y}\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\lambda-L}}. (3.7)

In particular, if τ=0\tau=0, then ‖∇Φλ​(zt)‖=‖∇p​(zt)‖.{\|\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z_{t})\|=\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|}.

Game stationarity incurs a bias linear in τ\tau, whereas the envelope gradient incurs a bias proportional to τ\sqrt{\tau}. These different dependences determine the two regularization choices in the concave case.

We count one full first-order oracle call at (x,y)(x,y) as returning (∇xf​(x,y),∇yf​(x,y))(\nabla_{x}f(x,y),\nabla_{y}f(x,y)). After one call at (x0,y0)(x_{0},y_{0}), each iteration queries only the predicted and corrected pairs. The corrected-point gradient is used for the momentum update and StS_{t}, then cached for the next prediction. Thus TT iterations require at most 1+2​T1+2T calls; the regularization terms are computed explicitly.

4 Convergence and Complexity Analysis

We first establish the Lyapunov and residual estimates shared by both regimes. We then present the NC–SC and NC–C complexity bounds in Sections 4.1 and 4.2, respectively, and give a common fixed-center warm-up refinement in Section 4.3. The common descent proof is in Appendices 8–9; the initialization, output, and complexity arguments are collected in Appendix 10.

Common Lyapunov estimates.

Throughout this section, we set λ=2​L\lambda=2L and fix τ≥0\tau\geq 0 such that 0<μy≤L0<\mu_{y}\leq L. The center update decreases pp up to an error proportional to ‖xt+1−x⋆​(zt)‖2\|x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\|^{2}. Since the algorithm makes only one auxiliary update before moving the center, this error must be controlled together with the auxiliary dynamics. The state at index aa need not have zero normal-cone or momentum variables.

To turn the aggregate estimates in Lemma 4.3 into output guarantees, Algorithm 1 selects the corrected pair minimizing the computable quantity StS_{t} for GS and samples a center uniformly for OS. Lemma 3.2 then transfers the corresponding bounds to the original problem. Neither rule evaluates ∇p​(zt)\nabla p(z_{t}) or solves an auxiliary saddle problem exactly.

4.1 Nonconvex–strongly concave complexity results

When μ>0\mu>0, taking τ=0\tau=0 gives p=Φ2​Lp=\Phi_{2L}. The two output rules give the following OS and GS guarantees for the constrained problem. Write κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu, and let Δ0\Delta_{0} denote the initial energy Δτ\Delta_{\tau} in (4.9) evaluated at τ=0\tau=0.

Theorem 4.2 (Nonconvex–strongly concave optimization-stationarity complexity).

Suppose that Assumption 2.1 holds with μ>0\mu>0. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, let τ=0\tau=0, μy=μ\mu_{y}=\mu, and λ=2​L\lambda=2L, and choose the remaining parameters as in (4.3). Run Algorithm 1 for

T=max⁡{1,⌈128​L​Δ0β​ε2⌉}T=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{128L\Delta_{0}}{\beta\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil\right\} (4.15)

iterations. The random center returned by Algorithm 1 satisfies

𝔼​‖∇Φ2​L​(zout)‖2≤ε2.\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}. (4.16)
Remark 4.1.

For fixed Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0, as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, the first-order oracle complexity of Theorem 4.2 is

O⁡(κ​L​Δ0​ε−2).O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}\right). (4.17)
Theorem 4.3 (Nonconvex–strongly concave game-stationarity complexity).

Under the assumptions and parameter choices of Theorem 4.2, run Algorithm 1 for TT iterations, with TT given by (4.15). The deterministic game output satisfies

ℛ⁡(xout,yout)≤ε.\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\varepsilon. (4.18)
Remark 4.2.

For fixed Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0, as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, the first-order oracle complexity of Theorem 4.3 is

O⁡(κ​L​Δ0​ε−2).O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}\right). (4.19)

The two theorems use the same trajectory and iteration budget; only the output rule differs. Section 4.3 sharpens the leading initialization dependence from Δ0\Delta_{0} to the value-function gap by adding a fixed-center warm-up. No warm-up is needed for the baseline bounds above.

O⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3).O\!\left(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}\right). (4.42)
Corollary 4.4 (Warm-started NC–C game stationarity).

Suppose that μ=0\mu=0. Choose τ\tau as in (4.26) and set η=τ​DY2\eta=\tau D_{Y}^{2}. Algorithm 2 returns a deterministic pair satisfying

ℛ⁡(xout,yout)≤ε.\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\leq\varepsilon. (4.43)

The full query bound is again (4.38), with B0,τ,η=Δϕ+3​τ​DY2/2B_{0,\tau,\eta}=\Delta_{\phi}+3\tau D_{Y}^{2}/2. For a fixed instance with Δϕ>0\Delta_{\phi}>0, its leading order as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 is

O(L3/2DY1/2Δϕε−5/2).O\!\left(L^{3/2}D_{Y}^{1/2}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-5/2}\right). (4.44)
Remark 4.5 (Tolerance and budget information).

The positive tolerance η\eta is distinct from the perturbation parameter τ\tau. In the NC–C case, η=τ​DY2\eta=\tau D_{Y}^{2} recovers the original warm-up target; in the NC–SC case, τ=0\tau=0 and this target must be replaced by a positive tolerance. The choice η=ε2/L\eta=\varepsilon^{2}/L is valid even when Δϕ=0\Delta_{\phi}=0. If only a known bound Δ¯≥Δϕ\overline{\Delta}\geq\Delta_{\phi} is available, it may replace Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} in the budget and complexity statements. In particular, for NC–SC and Δ¯>0\overline{\Delta}>0, the alternative η=Δ¯\eta=\overline{\Delta} and B=2​Δ¯B=2\overline{\Delta} gives

N=O⁡(κ​[L​Δ¯ε2+1+log⁡max⁡{1,H¯μ/Δ¯}]),N=O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa}\left[\frac{L\overline{\Delta}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+1+\log\max\{1,\overline{H}_{\mu}/\overline{\Delta}\}\right]\right), (4.45)

whose warm-up length is independent of ε\varepsilon. Neither version evaluates the envelope or its infimum. The additive terms in the full bounds cannot be discarded for a zero gap or unbounded initialization errors.

5 Lower Bound for Optimization Stationarity

5.1 Problem class and oracle model

Fix L,Δ,DY>0L,\Delta,D_{Y}>0. Consider instances of (2.1) with X=ℝdxX=\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, a nonempty compact convex dual set Y⊂ℝdyY\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} containing the origin, and a globally continuously differentiable objective function f:ℝdx+dy→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}+d_{y}}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying

‖∇f​(w)−∇f​(w′)‖≤L​‖w−w′‖(w,w′∈ℝdx+dy),f⁡(x,⋅)​ is concave,diam⁡(Y)≤DY,ϕ⁡(0)−infxϕ⁡(x)≤Δ.\begin{gathered}\|\nabla f(w)-\nabla f(w^{\prime})\|\leq L\|w-w^{\prime}\|\quad(w,w^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}+d_{y}}),\\ f(x,\cdot)\text{ is concave},\qquad\diam(Y)\leq D_{Y},\qquad\phi(0)-\inf_{x}\phi(x)\leq\Delta.\end{gathered} (5.1)

Let Δϕ:=ϕ⁡(0)−infxϕ⁡(x)≤Δ\Delta_{\phi}:=\phi(0)-\inf_{x}\phi(x)\leq\Delta denote the actual initial gap. The dimensions are not fixed in advance. In particular, global smoothness in (5.1) is stronger than the product-domain smoothness required in Assumption 2.1. Since ϕ\phi is LL-weakly convex and bounded below, Φ2​L\Phi_{2L} under the convention (2.6) is differentiable. The pointwise OS target is

‖∇Φ2​L​(xout)‖≤ε.\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|\leq\varepsilon. (5.2)
Definition 5.1 (Projected zero-respecting first-order method).

Let 𝒵=ℝdx×Y\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times Y and F⁡(x,y)=(∇xf​(x,y),−∇yf​(x,y))F(x,y)=(\nabla_{x}f(x,y),-\nabla_{y}f(x,y)). A deterministic method starts at w0=0w^{0}=0 and queries FF at feasible points wt∈𝒵w^{t}\in\mathcal{Z}. It is projected zero-respecting if each subsequent query satisfies

wt+1=Π𝒵​(at+1),supp⁡(at+1)⊆⋃s=0t(supp⁡(ws)∪supp⁡(F⁡(ws))).\begin{gathered}w^{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(a^{t+1}),\\ \supp(a^{t+1})\subseteq\bigcup_{s=0}^{t}\bigl(\supp(w^{s})\cup\supp(F(w^{s}))\bigr).\end{gathered} (5.3)

After TT queries, at w0,…,wT−1w^{0},\ldots,w^{T-1}, its output must also satisfy

wout=Π𝒵​(aout),supp⁡(aout)⊆⋃s=0T−1(supp⁡(ws)∪supp⁡(F⁡(ws))).\begin{gathered}w^{\mathrm{out}}=\Pi_{\mathcal{Z}}(a^{\mathrm{out}}),\\ \supp(a^{\mathrm{out}})\subseteq\bigcup_{s=0}^{T-1}\bigl(\supp(w^{s})\cup\supp(F(w^{s}))\bigr).\end{gathered} (5.4)

A primal-only output is permitted if it is the first block of such a woutw^{\mathrm{out}}. For T=0T=0, the union is empty and the output is the origin. Complexity counts first-order oracle calls; projections are not charged.

The output restriction is part of the model. Accordingly, the result does not cover methods that introduce arbitrary unexplored coordinates or arbitrary changes of basis.

Remark 5.1 (Randomized outputs).

The support induction and Moreau-gradient barrier hold pathwise. For randomized methods satisfying (5.3)–(5.4) almost surely, any fixed query budget T<M⁡(n+1)T<M(n+1) therefore gives

𝔼​‖∇Φ2​L​(xout)‖>2​ε,𝔼​‖∇Φ2​L​(xout)‖2>4​ε2.\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|>2\varepsilon,\qquad\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(x^{\mathrm{out}})\|^{2}>4\varepsilon^{2}.

Thus the lower bound also holds for the expected-norm OS criterion in Definition 2.1 and the expected squared-norm criterion in Theorem 4.4, at a fixed total query budget.

Remark 5.2 (Matching the upper bound).

The leading OS upper bound (4.42) for Algorithm 2 matches the lower bound in Theorem 5.1 in its L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3} dependence within the class of projected zero-respecting methods. The additional terms in (4.38) are lower order for each fixed instance with Δϕ>0\Delta_{\phi}>0 as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0. Appendix 11.4 verifies the initialization and oracle-class conditions required for this comparison.

6 Numerical Experiments

We provide two numerical examples to illustrate the empirical behavior of the proposed method. We compare our method with GDA, AGP, Smoothed GDA (SGDA), and Perturbed Smoothed GDA (PSGDA). Performance is measured against the number of full-gradient oracle calls; for the Waterbirds experiment, we additionally report elapsed time.

6.1 Dirac-GAN

We first consider the Dirac-GAN game used in Xu et al. (2023),

minx∈ℝ⁡maxy∈ℝ⁡f⁡(x,y)=−log⁡(1+e−x​y)+log⁡2.\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}}f(x,y)=-\log(1+e^{-xy})+\log 2. (6.1)

Its stationary point is (0,0)(0,0). We measure convergence by

dt=xt2+yt2.d_{t}=\sqrt{x_{t}^{2}+y_{t}^{2}}.

We compare Ours with GDA, AGP, SGDA, and PSGDA. All methods start from (x0,y0)=(1,1)(x_{0},y_{0})=(1,1). Figure 1 reports the distance to the stationary point against full-gradient oracle calls and shows the corresponding trajectories in the (x,y)(x,y) plane.

Figure 1(a) shows that Ours converges rapidly to the stationary point. It first reaches and remains below d=10−2d=10^{-2} after 77 oracle calls, compared with 99 calls for PSGDA, 1515 calls for AGP, and 2323 calls for SGDA. For the more stringent threshold d=10−8d=10^{-8}, Ours reaches the threshold after 1313 calls, while PSGDA requires 2525 calls in the displayed run.

Figure 1(b) further illustrates the different dynamics of the methods. Ours approaches the origin directly and rapidly, whereas GDA exhibits pronounced rotational behavior. Taken together, the two panels show that the proposed method outperforms all compared baselines in this example: it reaches the reported distance thresholds with fewer oracle calls and follows a more direct trajectory toward the stationary point.

6.2 Waterbirds Group DRO

We next consider a group distributionally robust optimization problem based on the Waterbirds dataset Sagawa et al. (2020):

min‖θ‖2≤5⁡maxy∈Δ4⁡f⁡(θ,y)=∑g=14yg|Ig|​∑j∈Iglog⁡(1+e−bj​sθ​(aj)).\min_{\|\theta\|_{2}\leq 5}\max_{y\in\Delta_{4}}f(\theta,y)=\sum_{g=1}^{4}\frac{y_{g}}{|I_{g}|}\sum_{j\in I_{g}}\log\!\left(1+e^{-b_{j}s_{\theta}(a_{j})}\right). (6.2)

Here Δ4={y≥0:𝟏⊤​y=1}\Delta_{4}=\{y\geq 0:\mathbf{1}^{\top}y=1\}, IgI_{g} indexes the samples in group gg, and bj∈{−1,1}b_{j}\in\{-1,1\} is the bird label. The four groups are determined by the bird labels and backgrounds. We use fixed ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 features followed by a fixed projection to ℝ32\mathbb{R}^{32}. The classifier is

sθ​(a)=v⊤​tanh⁡(W⊤​a+u)+c,θ=(vec⁡(W),u,v,c)∈ℝ137,s_{\theta}(a)=v^{\top}\tanh(W^{\top}a+u)+c,\qquad\theta=(\operatorname{vec}(W),u,v,c)\in\mathbb{R}^{137},

where W∈ℝ32×4W\in\mathbb{R}^{32\times 4}, u,v∈ℝ4u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{4}, and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. The resulting objective is nonconvex in θ\theta and linear in yy.

With X={θ:‖θ‖2≤5}X=\{\theta:\|\theta\|_{2}\leq 5\}, we evaluate the methods using the projected first-order residual

ℛproj​(θ,y)=‖θ−ΠX​(θ−∇θf)‖22+‖y−ΠΔ4​(y+∇yf)‖22.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{proj}}(\theta,y)=\sqrt{\|\theta-\Pi_{X}(\theta-\nabla_{\theta}f)\|_{2}^{2}+\|y-\Pi_{\Delta_{4}}(y+\nabla_{y}f)\|_{2}^{2}}. (6.3)

We compare Ours with GDA, AGP, SGDA, and PSGDA from the same initial point and on the same data split. Figure 2 reports the best projected residual against both full-gradient oracle calls and elapsed time.

Figure 2(a) shows that the proposed method achieves the smallest projected residual among all compared methods. After 10011001 full-gradient oracle calls, Ours reaches 3.457×10−43.457\times 10^{-4}, compared with 1.520×10−31.520\times 10^{-3} for PSGDA, 8.269×10−38.269\times 10^{-3} for SGDA, 2.797×10−22.797\times 10^{-2} for AGP, and 1.914×10−11.914\times 10^{-1} for GDA.

The elapsed-time curves in Figure 2(b) show a similar trend: the proposed method decreases the residual rapidly and attains the best final residual among the compared methods. Thus, on this Waterbirds instance, the proposed method outperforms all compared baselines under both the full-gradient-oracle-call and elapsed-time comparisons, achieving the smallest projected residual in each case.

7 Conclusions

This work closes the complexity gap between single-loop and multi-loop first-order methods for smooth nonconvex–concave minimax optimization under both optimization stationarity (OS) and game stationarity (GS). The algorithmic contribution lies in coordinating projected extragradient steps, dual momentum, and proximal-center evolution within a single loop. The theoretical contribution is a Lyapunov analysis that jointly controls optimization progress and saddle-point tracking, together with a lower-bound construction certifying the sharpness of the OS guarantee.

For OS, the fixed-center warm-up converts the initialization-dependent bound O⁡(L2​DY​Δ¯0​ε−3)O(L^{2}D_{Y}\bar{\Delta}_{0}\varepsilon^{-3}) into the leading complexity O⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3)O(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}), relegating the initial-gradient dependence to an additive lower-order cost. Our globally smooth hard instances require Ω⁡(L2​DY​Δϕ​ε−3)\Omega(L^{2}D_{Y}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-3}) queries from projected zero-respecting first-order methods, even when admissible randomized outputs are allowed at a fixed query budget. Thus, on the common initialization class, the upper and lower bounds agree up to a constant factor in all displayed parameters. This establishes optimality of the leading warm-started OS complexity within the stated oracle class, beyond merely identifying the sharp ε−3\varepsilon^{-3} exponent.

For GS, the leading bound O(L3/2DY1/2Δϕε−5/2)O(L^{3/2}D_{Y}^{1/2}\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-5/2}) shows that the best-known multi-loop rate can be attained through elementary single-loop updates, without a logarithmic factor in the leading term. To our knowledge, no previous single-loop method achieves this bound for general smooth nonconvex–concave problems. Dual strong concavity further yields O⁡(κ​L​Δ0​ε−2)O(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2}) complexity for both criteria; after warm-up, the leading term becomes O⁡(κ​L​Δϕ​ε−2)O(\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{\phi}\varepsilon^{-2}), matching the known lower-bound rate for value-gradient stationarity in the corresponding unconstrained oracle models. These warm-started leading bounds apply for fixed problem and initialization quantities with Δϕ>0\Delta_{\phi}>0 as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0.

The resulting picture is that sharp complexity guarantees need not rely on nested auxiliary solvers: a suitably coordinated single-loop dynamics can attain them, with oracle optimality established for OS. Natural next steps include stochastic extensions, treatment of unbounded dual domains, and lower bounds for broader first-order oracle classes.

8 Saddle-Point Sensitivity and Center Descent

Throughout this appendix, Assumption 2.1 holds, λ=2​L\lambda=2L, 0<μy=μ+τ≤L0<\mu_{y}=\mu+\tau\leq L, and the parameters are given by (4.3).

8.1 Saddle-point sensitivity

We first estimate how the saddle point changes with the center. For z,z′∈ℝnz,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, write δ​z=z′−z\delta z=z^{\prime}-z, δ​x⋆=x⋆​(z′)−x⋆​(z)\delta x^{\star}=x^{\star}(z^{\prime})-x^{\star}(z), and δ​y⋆=y⋆​(z′)−y⋆​(z)\delta y^{\star}=y^{\star}(z^{\prime})-y^{\star}(z). Adding the variational inequalities at the two saddle points and using LL-strong convexity in xx, μy\mu_{y}-strong concavity in yy, and Young’s inequality gives

L​‖δ​x⋆‖2+μy​‖δ​y⋆‖2\displaystyle L\|\delta x^{\star}\|^{2}+\mu_{y}\|\delta y^{\star}\|^{2} ≤2​L​⟨δ​z,δ​x⋆⟩≤L2​‖δ​x⋆‖2+2​L​‖δ​z‖2.\displaystyle\leq 2L\langle\delta z,\delta x^{\star}\rangle\leq\frac{L}{2}\|\delta x^{\star}\|^{2}+2L\|\delta z\|^{2}. (8.1)

Consequently,

‖x⋆​(z′)−x⋆​(z)‖\displaystyle\|x^{\star}(z^{\prime})-x^{\star}(z)\| ≤2​‖z′−z‖,\displaystyle\leq 2\|z^{\prime}-z\|, (8.2)
‖y⋆​(z′)−y⋆​(z)‖\displaystyle\|y^{\star}(z^{\prime})-y^{\star}(z)\| ≤2​Lμy​‖z′−z‖.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{2L}{\mu_{y}}}\|z^{\prime}-z\|.

8.2 Smoothness of the auxiliary envelope

Combining the first estimate in (8.2) with (3.2) yields

∇p​(z)\displaystyle\nabla p(z) =2​L​(z−x⋆​(z)),\displaystyle=2L(z-x^{\star}(z)), (8.3)
‖∇p​(z′)−∇p​(z)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla p(z^{\prime})-\nabla p(z)\| ≤6​L​‖z′−z‖.\displaystyle\leq 6L\|z^{\prime}-z\|.

8.3 Proof of Lemma 4.1

Proof.

The center update and (3.2) give

zt+1−zt\displaystyle z_{t+1}-z_{t} =β⁡(xt+1−zt)\displaystyle=\beta(x_{t+1}-z_{t}) (8.4)
=β⁡[xt+1−x⋆​(zt)+x⋆​(zt)−zt]\displaystyle=\beta\bigl[x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})+x^{\star}(z_{t})-z_{t}\bigr]
=β(xt+1−x⋆(zt)−12​L∇p(zt)).\displaystyle=\beta\left(x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})-\frac{1}{2L}\nabla p(z_{t})\right).

In particular,

‖zt+1−zt‖2≤2​β2​‖xt+1−x⋆​(zt)‖2+β22​L2​‖∇p​(zt)‖2.\|z_{t+1}-z_{t}\|^{2}\leq 2\beta^{2}\|x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{\beta^{2}}{2L^{2}}\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|^{2}. (8.5)

By 6​L6L-smoothness and Young’s inequality,

⟨∇p​(zt),xt+1−x⋆​(zt)⟩≤18​L​‖∇p​(zt)‖2+2​L​‖xt+1−x⋆​(zt)‖2,\langle\nabla p(z_{t}),x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\rangle\leq\frac{1}{8L}\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|^{2}+2L\|x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\|^{2},

we obtain

p⁡(zt+1)−p⁡(zt)\displaystyle p(z_{t+1})-p(z_{t}) ≤⟨∇p​(zt),zt+1−zt⟩+3​L​‖zt+1−zt‖2\displaystyle\leq\langle\nabla p(z_{t}),z_{t+1}-z_{t}\rangle+3L\|z_{t+1}-z_{t}\|^{2}
≤−βL​(38−32​β)​‖∇p​(zt)‖2\displaystyle\leq-\frac{\beta}{L}\left(\frac{3}{8}-\frac{3}{2}\beta\right)\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|^{2}
+β​L​(2+6​β)​‖xt+1−x⋆​(zt)‖2.\displaystyle\quad+\beta L(2+6\beta)\|x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\|^{2}.

By (4.3), μy≤L\mu_{y}\leq L, and LG≥3​LL_{G}\geq 3L, we have 0<β≤2/(3⋅64⋅4096)<1/120<\beta\leq\sqrt{2}/(3\cdot 64\cdot 4096)<1/12. Consequently, 3/8−3​β/2≥1/43/8-3\beta/2\geq 1/4 and 2+6​β≤5/22+6\beta\leq 5/2, which gives (4.4). ∎

The squared-distance term in this bound is absorbed by the decrease in the auxiliary error established in the next appendix.

The parameters are those in (4.3), with λ=2​L\lambda=2L and 0<μy=μ+τ≤L0<\mu_{y}=\mu+\tau\leq L. The proof separates the value-function change from the change in the auxiliary tracking error:

9.2 Positivity and fixed-center dissipation

We use the potential function defined in (4.2).

Lemma 9.2.

For every state ww admitted by the definition in (4.2),

ℰz​(w)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{z}(w)
≥12​L​‖∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ‖2+2​L​μy32​‖x−x⋆​(z)‖2+μy2​‖y−y⋆​(z)‖2\displaystyle\geq{}\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi\|^{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\|x-x^{\star}(z)\|^{2}+\frac{\mu_{y}}{2}\|y-y^{\star}(z)\|^{2}
+1L​‖−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n−v−2​L​μy32​(y−y⋆​(z))‖2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{L}\left\|-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n-v-\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}(y-y^{\star}(z))\right\|^{2}. (9.11)

Moreover,

⟨−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n,y−y⋆​(z)⟩+G⁡(x,y,z)−G⋆​(z)≥L2​‖x−x⋆​(z)‖2+μy2​‖y−y⋆​(z)‖2.\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n,y-y^{\star}(z)\rangle+G(x,y;z)-G^{\star}(z)\geq\frac{L}{2}\|x-x^{\star}(z)\|^{2}+\frac{\mu_{y}}{2}\|y-y^{\star}(z)\|^{2}. (9.12)
Proof.

Since ⟨n,y−y⋆​(z)⟩≥0\langle n,y-y^{\star}(z)\rangle\geq 0, combining the two inequalities proves (9.12).

Completing the square in (4.2), we obtain

ℰz​(w)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{z}(w)
=−16​L−2​L​μy16​L​(G⁡(x,y,z)−G⋆​(z))+1L​‖∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ‖2\displaystyle={}-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{16L}\bigl(G(x,y;z)-G^{\star}(z)\bigr)+\frac{1}{L}\|\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi\|^{2}
+2​L​μy16​L​⟨−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n,y−y⋆​(z)⟩\displaystyle+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{16L}\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n,y-y^{\star}(z)\rangle
+1L​‖−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n−v−2​L​μy32​(y−y⋆​(z))‖2+μy512​‖y−y⋆​(z)‖2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{L}\left\|-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n-v-\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}(y-y^{\star}(z))\right\|^{2}+\frac{\mu_{y}}{512}\|y-y^{\star}(z)\|^{2}. (9.15)

Substituting (9.14) and ⟨n,y−y⋆​(z)⟩≥0\langle n,y-y^{\star}(z)\rangle\geq 0 gives

ℰz​(w)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{z}(w)
≥−(G⁡(x,y,z)−G⋆​(z))+2​L​μy16​L​(G⁡(x,y⋆​(z),z)−G⋆​(z))+1L​‖∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ‖2\displaystyle\geq{}-\bigl(G(x,y;z)-G^{\star}(z)\bigr)+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{16L}\bigl(G(x,y^{\star}(z);z)-G^{\star}(z)\bigr)+\frac{1}{L}\|\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi\|^{2}
+1L​‖−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n−v−2​L​μy32​(y−y⋆​(z))‖2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{L}\left\|-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n-v-\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}(y-y^{\star}(z))\right\|^{2}. (9.16)

=G⁡(x,y,z)−12​L​‖∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ‖2+L2​‖a−x+∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξL‖2\displaystyle=G(x,y;z)-\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi\|^{2}+\frac{L}{2}\left\|a-x+\frac{\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi}{L}\right\|^{2}
≥G⁡(x,y,z)−12​L​‖∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ‖2.\displaystyle\geq G(x,y;z)-\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi\|^{2}.

whereas strong concavity at the saddle point gives

mina∈X⁡G⁡(a,y,z)≤G⁡(x⋆​(z),y,z)≤G⋆​(z)−μy2​‖y−y⋆​(z)‖2.\min_{a\in X}G(a,y;z)\leq G(x^{\star}(z),y;z)\leq G^{\star}(z)-\frac{\mu_{y}}{2}\|y-y^{\star}(z)\|^{2}.

Substituting this inequality and (9.13) into (9.16) proves (9.11). ∎

To relate the one-step change at a fixed center to its dissipation terms, we split the auxiliary subproblem error into three components:

Az​(w):=\displaystyle A_{z}(w):={} −16​L−2​L​μy32​(G⁡(x,y,z)−G⋆​(z))+12​‖∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ‖2,\displaystyle-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\bigl(G(x,y;z)-G^{\star}(z)\bigr)+\frac{1}{2}\|\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi\|^{2},

Cz​(w):=\displaystyle C_{z}(w):={} 2​L​μy32​⟨v,y−y⋆​(z)⟩+L​μy512​‖y−y⋆​(z)‖2+2​L​μy512​L​‖v‖2.\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\langle v,y-y^{\star}(z)\rangle+\frac{L\mu_{y}}{512}\|y-y^{\star}(z)\|^{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{512L}\|v\|^{2}. (9.17)

Then

Az​(w)+Bz​(w)+Cz​(w)=L2​[ℰz​(w)+2​L​μy256​L2​‖v‖2].A_{z}(w)+B_{z}(w)+C_{z}(w)=\frac{L}{2}\left[\mathcal{E}_{z}(w)+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{256L^{2}}\|v\|^{2}\right]. (9.18)

The third component contains the momentum cross term, the squared dual distance, and the kinetic energy. We estimate the changes of all three components jointly and retain the dissipation terms needed to control center movement.

We use the full one-step dissipation defined in (4.6).

To make the residual control explicit, define the two corrected residuals at the old center by

Pt+1\displaystyle P_{t+1} :=∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1,\displaystyle:=\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1}, (9.19)
Qt+1\displaystyle Q_{t+1} :=−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1−vt+1.\displaystyle:=-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1}-v_{t+1}.

The definition (4.6) gives the following lower bound:

𝒟zt​(wt+1,wt)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1},w_{t}) (9.20)
≥h4​‖Pt+1‖2+3​h​2​L​μy512​L​‖Qt+1‖2\displaystyle\geq\frac{h}{4}\|P_{t+1}\|^{2}+\frac{3h\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{512L}\|Q_{t+1}\|^{2}
+7​h​2​L​μy4096​L​‖vt+1‖2\displaystyle+\frac{7h\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{4096L}\|v_{t+1}\|^{2}
+h​2​L​μy​(16​L−2​L​μy)1024​‖xt+1−x⋆​(zt)‖2.\displaystyle+\frac{h\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}(16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}})}{1024}\|x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\|^{2}.

The omitted terms are nonnegative dual-tracking and projection-error terms. All displayed coefficients are positive because 0<μy≤L0<\mu_{y}\leq L. Thus the dissipation controls both blocks of the auxiliary stationarity residual, including the momentum needed to recover the dual residual Qt+1+vt+1Q_{t+1}+v_{t+1}, and the primal tracking error in the envelope descent.

Theorem 9.1.

For each iteration tt, the update from wtw_{t} to wt+1w_{t+1} at the fixed center ztz_{t} satisfies

ℰzt​(wt+1)−ℰzt​(wt)+2​L​μy256​L2​(‖vt+1‖2−‖vt‖2)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-\mathcal{E}_{z_{t}}(w_{t})+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{256L^{2}}\bigl(\|v_{t+1}\|^{2}-\|v_{t}\|^{2}\bigr) (9.21)
+h​2​L​μy32​[ℰzt​(wt+1)+2​L​μy256​L2​‖vt+1‖2]≤−𝒟zt​(wt+1,wt).\displaystyle+\frac{h\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\left[\mathcal{E}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})+\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{256L^{2}}\|v_{t+1}\|^{2}\right]\leq-\mathcal{D}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1},w_{t}).

Both terms in brackets are nonnegative by Lemma 9.2.

Proof.

By (9.18), it suffices to prove

Azt​(wt+1)−Azt​(wt)+Bzt​(wt+1)−Bzt​(wt)\displaystyle A_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-A_{z_{t}}(w_{t})+B_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-B_{z_{t}}(w_{t})
+Czt​(wt+1)−Czt​(wt)\displaystyle\quad+C_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-C_{z_{t}}(w_{t})
+h​2​L​μy32​[Azt​(wt+1)+Bzt​(wt+1)+Czt​(wt+1)]≤−L2​𝒟zt​(wt+1,wt).\displaystyle+\frac{h\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\bigl[A_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})+B_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})+C_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})\bigr]\leq-\frac{L}{2}\mathcal{D}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1},w_{t}). (9.22)

We first expand AztA_{z_{t}} and then add BztB_{z_{t}} and CztC_{z_{t}} in turn. The kinetic energy in CztC_{z_{t}} is kept as an explicit difference of squares and estimated using the momentum update in the final step.

Since ξt∈NX​(xt)\xi_{t}\in N_{X}(x_{t}) and nt+1∈NY​(yt+1)n_{t+1}\in N_{Y}(y_{t+1}),

⟨ξt,xt+1−xt⟩≤0,⟨nt+1,yt+1−yt⟩≥0.\langle\xi_{t},x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle\leq 0,\qquad\langle n_{t+1},y_{t+1}-y_{t}\rangle\geq 0.

+⟨∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)+ξt,xt+1−xt⟩+L2​‖xt+1−xt‖2,\displaystyle\quad+\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})+\xi_{t},x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|x_{t+1}-x_{t}\|^{2},

+⟨−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1,yt+1−yt⟩−μy2​‖yt+1−yt‖2.\displaystyle\quad+\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1},y_{t+1}-y_{t}\rangle-\frac{\mu_{y}}{2}\|y_{t+1}-y_{t}\|^{2}.

It follows that

−⟨−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1,yt+1−yt⟩\displaystyle-\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1},y_{t+1}-y_{t}\rangle
+L2​‖xt+1−xt‖2+μy2​‖yt+1−yt‖2.\displaystyle+\frac{L}{2}\|x_{t+1}-x_{t}\|^{2}+\frac{\mu_{y}}{2}\|y_{t+1}-y_{t}\|^{2}. (9.23)

The difference of squares and the cross term in the xx variable satisfy

12​(‖∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1‖2−‖∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)+ξt‖2)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\|\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1}\|^{2}-\|\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})+\xi_{t}\|^{2}\bigr)
−16​L−2​L​μy32​⟨∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)+ξt,xt+1−xt⟩\displaystyle-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})+\xi_{t},x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle
−L⁡(16​L−2​L​μy)64​‖xt+1−xt‖2\displaystyle-\frac{L(16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}})}{64}\|x_{t+1}-x_{t}\|^{2}
=⟨∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1,∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1−∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)−ξt⟩\displaystyle=\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1},\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1}-\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})-\xi_{t}\rangle
−16​L−2​L​μy32​⟨∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1,xt+1−xt⟩\displaystyle-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1},x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle
−12​‖∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1−∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)−ξt−16​L−2​L​μy32​(xt+1−xt)‖2\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\begin{aligned} &\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1}\\ &-\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})-\xi_{t}-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}(x_{t+1}-x_{t})\end{aligned}\right\|^{2}
−L⁡(128​L−μy)1024​‖xt+1−xt‖2.\displaystyle-\frac{L(128L-\mu_{y})}{1024}\|x_{t+1}-x_{t}\|^{2}. (9.24)

The last term is nonpositive because 0<μy≤L0<\mu_{y}\leq L. Multiplying (9.23) by −16​L−2​L​μy32-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32} and using (9.24) bounds the function-value term and the squared xx-residual in the potential.

Specifically, dropping the last term in (9.24) yields

Azt​(wt+1)−Azt​(wt)\displaystyle A_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-A_{z_{t}}(w_{t})
≤−16​L−2​L​μy32​⟨∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1,xt+1−xt⟩\displaystyle\leq-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1},x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle
+16​L−2​L​μy32​⟨−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1,yt+1−yt⟩\displaystyle+\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1},y_{t+1}-y_{t}\rangle
+⟨∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1,∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1−∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)−ξt⟩\displaystyle+\left\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1},\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1}-\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})-\xi_{t}\right\rangle
−12​‖∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+ξt+1−∇xG​(xt,yt,zt)−ξt−16​L−2​L​μy32​(xt+1−xt)‖2\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\left\|\begin{aligned} &\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\xi_{t+1}\\ &-\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})-\xi_{t}-\frac{16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{32}(x_{t+1}-x_{t})\end{aligned}\right\|^{2}
−μy​(16​L−2​L​μy)64​‖yt+1−yt‖2.\displaystyle-\frac{\mu_{y}(16L-\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}})}{64}\|y_{t+1}-y_{t}\|^{2}. (9.25)

Step 2: Jointly estimating the increments of AztA_{z_{t}} and BztB_{z_{t}}. The difference-of-squares identity gives

Bzt​(wt+1)−Bzt​(wt)\displaystyle B_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1})-B_{z_{t}}(w_{t})
=‖−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1−vt+1‖2\displaystyle={}\left\|-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1}-v_{t+1}\right\|^{2}
+⟨−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1−vt+1,∇yG​(xt,yt,zt)−nt+vt⟩\displaystyle+\left\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1}-v_{t+1},\nabla_{y}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})-n_{t}+v_{t}\right\rangle
−12​‖−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+nt+1−vt+1+∇yG​(xt,yt,zt)−nt+vt‖2.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\left\|-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+n_{t+1}-v_{t+1}+\nabla_{y}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t})-n_{t}+v_{t}\right\|^{2}. (9.26)

Applying strong convexity in xx at the two endpoints yields

G⁡(xt,yt+1,zt)\displaystyle G(x_{t},y_{t+1};z_{t}) ≥G⁡(xt+1,yt+1,zt)−⟨∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt),xt+1−xt⟩+L2​‖xt+1−xt‖2.\displaystyle\geq G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})-\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t}),x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|x_{t+1}-x_{t}\|^{2}.

Strong concavity in yy gives

Adding the first two inequalities gives a lower bound for the same mixed difference that is bounded from above by the sum of the last two inequalities. Eliminating the function values yields

⟨∇xG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)−∇xG​(xt,yt,zt),xt+1−xt⟩\displaystyle\langle\nabla_{x}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})-\nabla_{x}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t}),x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle
+⟨−∇yG​(xt+1,yt+1,zt)+∇yG​(xt,yt,zt),yt+1−yt⟩\displaystyle+\langle-\nabla_{y}G(x_{t+1},y_{t+1};z_{t})+\nabla_{y}G(x_{t},y_{t};z_{t}),y_{t+1}-y_{t}\rangle
≥L​‖xt+1−xt‖2+μy​‖yt+1−yt‖2.\displaystyle\geq L\|x_{t+1}-x_{t}\|^{2}+\mu_{y}\|y_{t+1}-y_{t}\|^{2}.

By monotonicity of the normal cones,

⟨ξt+1−ξt,xt+1−xt⟩≥0,⟨nt+1−nt,yt+1−yt⟩≥0.\langle\xi_{t+1}-\xi_{t},x_{t+1}-x_{t}\rangle\geq 0,\qquad\langle n_{t+1}-n_{t},y_{t+1}-y_{t}\rangle\geq 0.

Adding these inequalities gives

Proof of Lemma 4.2.

The dissipation in (4.6) is nonnegative. Dropping the term −𝒟zt(wt+1,wt)/2-\mathcal{D}_{z_{t}}(w_{t+1},w_{t})/2 from Lemma 9.4 gives (4.5). ∎

9.4 Proof of the unified Lyapunov descent

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

By (2.4) and ‖y‖≤DY\|y\|\leq D_{Y},

infzp⁡(z)≥infx∈Xϕ⁡(x)−τ​DY22>−∞.\inf_{z}p(z)\geq\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x)-\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{2}>-\infty.

Add the center-descent estimate of Lemma 4.1 to the auxiliary dissipation estimate of Lemma 9.4, namely (4.4) and (9.62). The coefficients of the primal tracking term ‖xt+1−x⋆​(zt)‖2\|x_{t+1}-x^{\star}(z_{t})\|^{2} are −5βL/2-5\beta L/2 and 5​β​L/25\beta L/2, and hence cancel. β8​L−β4​L=−β8​L.\frac{\beta}{8L}-\frac{\beta}{4L}=-\frac{\beta}{8L}.

The definition (4.1) now gives (4.7). Dropping the nonpositive dissipation term yields (4.8). ∎

10 From Lyapunov Descent to Complexity Bounds

We first establish the stationarity transfer and aggregate residual bounds. A common initialization calculation is then used by the baseline NC–SC and NC–C proofs and by the unified warm-up analysis. The fixed-center contraction and moving-center descent themselves remain in Appendix 9.

10.1 Transfer to the original problem

Proof of Lemma 3.2.

By Lemma 3.1 and the definition of distance to a set,

dist⁡(0,∇xf​(xt+1,yt+1)+NX​(xt+1))\displaystyle\dist\bigl(0,\nabla_{x}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+N_{X}(x_{t+1})\bigr)
≤‖∇xf​(xt+1,yt+1)+ξt+1‖,\displaystyle\qquad\leq\|\nabla_{x}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+\xi_{t+1}\|,
dist⁡(0,−∇yf​(xt+1,yt+1)+NY​(yt+1))\displaystyle\dist\bigl(0,-\nabla_{y}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+N_{Y}(y_{t+1})\bigr)
≤‖−∇yf​(xt+1,yt+1)+nt+1‖.\displaystyle\qquad\leq\|-\nabla_{y}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+n_{t+1}\|.

Consequently,

ℛ⁡(xt+1,yt+1)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})
≤‖(∇xf​(xt+1,yt+1)+ξt+1−∇yf​(xt+1,yt+1)+nt+1)‖\displaystyle\quad\leq\left\|\begin{pmatrix}\nabla_{x}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+\xi_{t+1}\\ -\nabla_{y}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+n_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}\right\|
=‖(∇xf​(xt+1,yt+1)+ξt+1−∇yf​(xt+1,yt+1)+τ​yt+1+nt+1)−(0τ​yt+1)‖\displaystyle\quad=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}\nabla_{x}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+\xi_{t+1}\\ -\nabla_{y}f(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+\tau y_{t+1}+n_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \tau y_{t+1}\end{pmatrix}\right\|
≤St+τ​‖yt+1‖≤St+τ​DY.\displaystyle\quad\leq\sqrt{S_{t}}+\tau\|y_{t+1}\|\leq\sqrt{S_{t}}+\tau D_{Y}.

The last line follows from the triangle inequality and ‖yt+1‖≤DY\|y_{t+1}\|\leq D_{Y}, proving (3.5).

To estimate the envelope-gradient bias, fix z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and recall x¯​(z)\bar{x}(z) from (2.7). Since ‖y‖≤DY\|y\|\leq D_{Y}, for every x∈Xx\in X,

0≤ϕ⁡(x)+λ2​‖x−z‖2−maxy∈Y⁡G⁡(x,y,z)≤τ​DY22.0\leq\phi(x)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|x-z\|^{2}-\max_{y\in Y}G(x,y;z)\leq\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{2}.

By the (λ−L)(\lambda-L)-strong convexity of the original proximal objective, this perturbation bound, and the optimality of x⋆​(z)x^{\star}(z), respectively,

λ−L2​‖x¯​(z)−x⋆​(z)‖2\displaystyle\frac{\lambda-L}{2}\|\bar{x}(z)-x^{\star}(z)\|^{2}
≤ϕ⁡(x⋆​(z))+λ2​‖x⋆​(z)−z‖2−ϕ⁡(x¯​(z))−λ2​‖x¯​(z)−z‖2\displaystyle\leq\phi(x^{\star}(z))+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|x^{\star}(z)-z\|^{2}-\phi(\bar{x}(z))-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\bar{x}(z)-z\|^{2}
≤maxy∈Y⁡G⁡(x⋆​(z),y,z)−maxy∈Y⁡G⁡(x¯​(z),y,z)+τ​DY22\displaystyle\leq\max_{y\in Y}G(x^{\star}(z),y;z)-\max_{y\in Y}G(\bar{x}(z),y;z)+\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{2}
≤τ​DY22.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{2}.

Therefore,

‖x¯​(z)−x⋆​(z)‖≤DY​τλ−L.\|\bar{x}(z)-x^{\star}(z)\|\leq D_{Y}\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\lambda-L}}. (10.1)

Equations (2.8) and (3.2) give

∇Φλ​(z)−∇p​(z)\displaystyle\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z)-\nabla p(z) =λ⁡(z−x¯​(z))−λ⁡(z−x⋆​(z))\displaystyle=\lambda(z-\bar{x}(z))-\lambda(z-x^{\star}(z))
=λ⁡(x⋆​(z)−x¯​(z)).\displaystyle=\lambda\bigl(x^{\star}(z)-\bar{x}(z)\bigr).

Taking norms and using (10.1), we obtain

‖∇Φλ​(z)−∇p​(z)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z)-\nabla p(z)\| =λ​‖x⋆​(z)−x¯​(z)‖\displaystyle=\lambda\|x^{\star}(z)-\bar{x}(z)\|
≤λ​DY​τλ−L.\displaystyle\leq\lambda D_{Y}\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\lambda-L}}.

This proves (3.6). Finally, at z=ztz=z_{t}, the triangle inequality gives

‖∇Φλ​(zt)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z_{t})\| ≤‖∇p​(zt)‖+‖∇Φλ​(zt)−∇p​(zt)‖\displaystyle\leq\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|+\|\nabla\Phi_{\lambda}(z_{t})-\nabla p(z_{t})\|
≤‖∇p​(zt)‖+λ​DY​τλ−L,\displaystyle\leq\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|+\lambda D_{Y}\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{\lambda-L}},

which proves (3.7). When τ=0\tau=0, the definitions give p=Φλp=\Phi_{\lambda}, so their gradients coincide. ∎

The estimates in this subsection hold for both regimes: μ≥0\mu\geq 0, τ≥0\tau\geq 0, and 0<μy=μ+τ≤L0<\mu_{y}=\mu+\tau\leq L. Define

ϕτ​(x):={maxy∈Y⁡{f⁡(x,y)−τ2​‖y‖2},x∈X,+∞,x∉X.\phi_{\tau}(x):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\max_{y\in Y}\left\{f(x,y)-\frac{\tau}{2}\|y\|^{2}\right\},&x\in X,\\ +\infty,&x\notin X.\end{cases} (10.10)

Thus ϕ0=ϕ\phi_{0}=\phi. Let HzH_{z} and H¯μ,τ\overline{H}_{\mu,\tau} be as in (4.29) and (4.30).

If z0=x0z_{0}=x_{0} and ξ0=n0=v0=0\xi_{0}=n_{0}=v_{0}=0, then

p⁡(x0)−infzp⁡(z)≤Δϕ+τ​DY22,p(x_{0})-\inf_{z}p(z)\leq\Delta_{\phi}+\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{2}, (10.11)

and

0≤Hx0​(w0)≤H¯μ,τ.0\leq H_{x_{0}}(w_{0})\leq\overline{H}_{\mu,\tau}. (10.12)

0≤ϕ⁡(x)−ϕτ​(x)≤τ​DY22.0\leq\phi(x)-\phi_{\tau}(x)\leq\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{2}. (10.13)

Hx0​(w0)=\displaystyle H_{x_{0}}(w_{0})={} (1−2​L​μy16​L)​[p⁡(x0)−f⁡(x0,y0)+τ2​‖y0‖2]\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{\sqrt{2L\mu_{y}}}{16L}\right)\left[p(x_{0})-f(x_{0},y_{0})+\frac{\tau}{2}\|y_{0}\|^{2}\right] (10.14)
+‖∇xf​(x0,y0)‖2+‖−∇yf​(x0,y0)+τ​y0‖2L+μy256​‖y0−y⋆​(x0)‖2.\displaystyle+\frac{\|\nabla_{x}f(x_{0},y_{0})\|^{2}+\|-\nabla_{y}f(x_{0},y_{0})+\tau y_{0}\|^{2}}{L}+\frac{\mu_{y}}{256}\|y_{0}-y^{\star}(x_{0})\|^{2}.

10.5 Baseline nonconvex–strongly concave complexity

Proof of Theorems 4.2 and 4.3.

Since τ=0\tau=0, Lemma 3.2 gives ‖∇Φ2​L​(zt)‖=‖∇p​(zt)‖\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{t})\|=\|\nabla p(z_{t})\|. Lemma 4.3 and (4.15) give

Sj≤32​L​Δ0β​T≤ε24,\displaystyle S_{j}\leq\frac{32L\Delta_{0}}{\beta T}\leq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4},
𝔼​‖∇Φ2​L​(zout)‖2≤8​L​Δ0β​T≤ε216.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z_{\rm out})\|^{2}\leq\frac{8L\Delta_{0}}{\beta T}\leq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{16}.

Combining the first inequality with (4.12) proves the game-stationarity claim. For τ=0\tau=0, the parameters satisfy

h=1192​L,β=2​μ/L786432=Θ⁡(μL).h=\frac{1}{192L},\qquad\beta=\frac{\sqrt{2\mu/L}}{786432}=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{L}}\right).

Under the full first-order oracle and gradient-caching convention in Section 3.2, initialization requires one query and each iteration requires two additional queries. Thus the total number is at most 1+2​T1+2T, which gives (4.17) and (4.19) as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 for fixed Δ0>0\Delta_{0}>0. ∎

Remark 10.1 (Budget from an initial-energy upper bound).

The budget does not require computing Δ0\Delta_{0} exactly. Given any known Δ¯0≥Δ0\overline{\Delta}_{0}\geq\Delta_{0}, choose instead

T=max⁡{1,⌈128​L​Δ¯0β​ε2⌉}.T=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{128L\overline{\Delta}_{0}}{\beta\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil\right\}. (10.15)

The conclusions of Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 then hold, and for fixed Δ¯0>0\overline{\Delta}_{0}>0 the complexity as ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 is

O⁡(Lμ​L​Δ¯0ε2)O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}\,\frac{L\overline{\Delta}_{0}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right) (10.16)

first-order oracle calls. This follows from the same proof by using Δ0≤Δ¯0\Delta_{0}\leq\overline{\Delta}_{0} in the two summation estimates. Thus an available upper bound suffices to prescribe the run length, without evaluating the envelope or its infimum.

Remark 10.2 (Optimal accuracy dependence under strong concavity).

The ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} accuracy dependence is optimal with the regularity and initialization bounds fixed. To see this, embed a smooth nonconvex minimization instance gg into f⁡(x,y)=g⁡(x)−μ​‖y‖2/2f(x,y)=g(x)-\mu\|y\|^{2}/2, with X=ℝnX=\mathbb{R}^{n} and a fixed compact convex YY containing 00. Then ϕ=g\phi=g, and the game residual controls ‖∇g​(x)‖\|\nabla g(x)\|. For OS, let u=proxg/(2​L)⁡(z)u=\operatorname{prox}_{g/(2L)}(z). Proximal optimality and smoothness give

∇Φ2​L​(z)=∇g​(u)=2​L​(z−u),‖∇g​(z)‖≤32​‖∇Φ2​L​(z)‖.\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z)=\nabla g(u)=2L(z-u),\qquad\|\nabla g(z)\|\leq\tfrac{3}{2}\|\nabla\Phi_{2L}(z)\|.

This pointwise inequality also transfers an expected squared-norm guarantee. Initialize z0=x0z_{0}=x_{0}, y0=0y_{0}=0, and the normal and momentum variables at zero. The definition of Δ0\Delta_{0} and the gradient-gap inequality imply

Δ0≤g⁡(x0)−infg+‖∇g​(x0)‖2L≤3​(g⁡(x0)−infg).\Delta_{0}\leq g(x_{0})-\inf g+\frac{\|\nabla g(x_{0})\|^{2}}{L}\leq 3\bigl(g(x_{0})-\inf g\bigr).

The smooth-minimization lower bound of Carmon et al. (2020) therefore applies under a common bounded initialization budget. This establishes optimality of the accuracy exponent, without asserting optimality of the condition-number dependence.

Remark 10.3 (Dependence on the condition number).

Writing κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu, Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 give a baseline gradient complexity upper bound of order 1+κ​L​Δ0​ε−21+\sqrt{\kappa}L\Delta_{0}\varepsilon^{-2} for each stated output criterion. Corollary 4.2 replaces Δ0\Delta_{0} in the leading term by Δϕ\Delta_{\phi}, with an additive initialization cost. An optimality comparison must retain both the stationarity criterion and the initialization quantity: lower bounds expressed through the gradient of the value function do not, by themselves, establish a matching lower bound for either guarantee stated here.

11 Lower-Bound Construction

We first establish the regularity of the base instance and its value function, then show how the oracle reveals the chain coordinates. A value-gradient barrier yields the Moreau-gradient barrier needed for Theorem 5.1. The final subsection verifies the initialization and oracle-class conditions for comparing the bounds. All constants in the base construction are independent of MM and nn.

Lemma 11.7 (Moreau-envelope gradient barrier).

Let c0=1/512c_{0}=1/512 and use the curvature convention

ΦM,n,2​L0​(x):=minu⁡{φM,n​(u)+L0​‖u−x‖2}.\Phi_{M,n,2L_{0}}(x):=\min_{u}\{\varphi_{M,n}(u)+L_{0}\|u-x\|^{2}\}.

‖∇ΦM,n,2​L0​(x)‖>c0.\|\nabla\Phi_{M,n,2L_{0}}(x)\|>c_{0}. (11.24)

Consequently, the output of every projected zero-respecting first-order algorithm after T<M⁡(n+1)T<M(n+1) queries satisfies (11.24).

Proof.

p=argminu{φM,n​(u)+L0​‖u−x‖2}p=\argmin_{u}\{\varphi_{M,n}(u)+L_{0}\|u-x\|^{2}\}

exists and is unique. Set d=∇ΦM,n,2​L0​(x)d=\nabla\Phi_{M,n,2L_{0}}(x). The Moreau-gradient identity and the proximal optimality condition give

d=2​L0​(x−p),0=∇φM,n​(p)+2​L0​(p−x).d=2L_{0}(x-p),\qquad 0=\nabla\varphi_{M,n}(p)+2L_{0}(p-x).

Thus d=∇φM,n​(p)d=\nabla\varphi_{M,n}(p) and p=x−d/(2​L0)p=x-d/(2L_{0}). If xM=0x_{M}=0 and ‖d‖≤c0\|d\|\leq c_{0}, then

|pM|=|dM|2​L0≤12​L0⋅512<12.|p_{M}|=\frac{|d_{M}|}{2L_{0}}\leq\frac{1}{2L_{0}\cdot 512}<\frac{1}{2}.

Lemma 11.6 then gives ‖d‖=‖∇φM,n​(p)‖≥1/256>c0\|d\|=\|\nabla\varphi_{M,n}(p)\|\geq 1/256>c_{0}, a contradiction. The output statement follows from Lemma 11.5. ∎

11.4 Initialization for the upper-bound comparison

On the scaled hard instance, initialization at the origin gives

∇xfsc​(0,0)=0,∇yfsc​(0,0)=ab​n​e1,ab​n≤L​DY4.\nabla_{x}f_{\mathrm{sc}}(0,0)=0,\qquad\nabla_{y}f_{\mathrm{sc}}(0,0)=\frac{a}{b\sqrt{n}}e_{1},\qquad\frac{a}{b\sqrt{n}}\leq\frac{LD_{Y}}{4}.

Substitution into (4.20) yields

Δ¯0≤Δ+38​L​DY2.\bar{\Delta}_{0}\leq\Delta+\frac{3}{8}LD_{Y}^{2}. (11.25)

For fixed L,Δ,DYL,\Delta,D_{Y}, Lemma 4.4 therefore bounds Δτ\Delta_{\tau} uniformly for 0<τ≤L0<\tau\leq L on the common class satisfying (5.1) and Δ¯0≤Δ+38​L​DY2\bar{\Delta}_{0}\leq\Delta+\tfrac{3}{8}LD_{Y}^{2}. The OS upper and lower bounds match in their ε−3\varepsilon^{-3} accuracy dependence on this class. If Δ≥L​DY2\Delta\geq LD_{Y}^{2}, the hard family also belongs to the common initialization class Δ¯0≤2​Δ\bar{\Delta}_{0}\leq 2\Delta, on which the leading dependence matches at order L2​Δ​DY​ε−3L^{2}\Delta D_{Y}\varepsilon^{-3}.

With all states initialized at zero, Algorithms 1 and 2 satisfy the oracle support restrictions on these domains. Their linear combinations, regularization gradients, momentum and center updates, and stored-output selection preserve revealed support. Projections preserve support by Lemma 11.1, as do their residuals. Each gradient evaluation counts as a query; the fixed-center warm-up and its transition to the main phase introduce no new coordinates.
